# forge-factory

forge-factory owns what a workspace is made of and what version everything agrees on. It generates the files that name both, so a version is written in one place and nowhere else.

## Verbs

| Verb | Does |
|---|---|
| `sync` | Materialise every generated file from the factory plus each repo's forge.yaml |
| `add <name> <url> <language...>` | Add a member, then sync |
| `bump <dependency> <version>` | Rewrite one version line, then sync |
| `checkout <revision>` | Read a revision from the state engine, put every member on its SHA, then sync |
| `status` | Report what on disk disagrees with the factory |
| `validate` | Parse the factory and print what it declares |

## Concepts

### The register

A dependency entry that is an object resolves from the register: the catalog of adoptable package versions, advanced by policy, written only by its own pipeline.

The local register checkout wins, like any member. A bare string stays a version written verbatim, exactly as before the register existed. Resolution is strict: a missing package fails loud and files a request for the register pipeline to answer, and a security advisory on a resolved version fails the sync whatever pins say - an advisory pierces every pin.

### Pins

A soft pin floors a track and retires itself once the register catches up. A hard pin freezes one consumer, visibly, and never blocks the register.

Every pin carries a reason - a pin without one is a config error, not a warning. Sync explains every standing pin, names the dead ones to remove, and a wraps template renders the resolved version into whatever the language file needs, so a rust inline table keeps its features and a python specifier keeps its operator.

### The factory file

forge-factory.yaml declares members, shared dependency versions, a language engine per language, and optionally a state engine.

Membership was declared five times before this and none of the five agreed. One file is the source and every other list is generated from it.

### Generated files are gitignored

go.work, the root Cargo.toml, pnpm-workspace.yaml, every go.mod, package.json and pyproject.toml are output.

A committed version file is a version written twice. Bumping a dependency then needs a pull request in every repo, which is the whole problem this tool exists to remove. Nothing generated is committed, so drift is impossible rather than detected.

See also: No lone clones

### No lone clones

A repo is built through the toolchain, never on its own.

That is what makes generated dependency files possible at all. forge-factory itself is the exception, because it is what materialises the files everything else needs.

### Two dependency lists

dependencies is what a package ships. devDependencies is what only the tests and the tooling need.

They are kept apart because a published package must not carry its test runner. Each becomes the right section of the right file per language.

### Language engines

One MCP engine per language answers what to write for that language.

forge-factory knows nothing about cargo, pnpm or uv. It asks an engine, writes what comes back, and keeps the gitignore in step. A new language is a new engine and no change here.

### Per-repo identity

The module path, package name and entry point come from that repo's forge.yaml factory block.

forge ignores keys it does not know, so the block costs that repo nothing and no new per-repo file exists. toolConfig travels verbatim into the generated file: pytest options, ruff rules and coverage omits are the repo's business and no factory declares them.

### The state engine

A revision is a tuple of repo commits that a pipeline proved. checkout puts every member on the SHAs that revision names.

forge-factory speaks the transport in forge-revision-spec and imports forge-ci nowhere. Either tool works alone, and swapping the state engine moves both.
